newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan car production jumps on weak yen, RV boom.
newsitem.headline: Japan car production jumps on weak yen, RV boom.

text.p: Three of Japan's five major carmakers reported on Monday that their domestic vehicle production jumped last year, driven by the weaker yen and a booming market for recreational models.
The figures could signal a shift in a long-standing trend for car makers to scale back their manufacturing in high-cost Japan and boost overseas output, industry sources said.

Japan's top carmaker Toyota Motor Corp said its domestic automobile production rose 7.5 percent in 1996 from a year earlier to 3.41 million units in 1996, helped by strong domestic demand for new models and higher exports.
The home market for recreational vehicles is booming as customers swap their sedate sedans for sporty alternatives.
"Higher domestic sales were mainly due to strong demand for new recreational vehicles like the Ipsum, the TwoAce Noah and the LiteAce Noah," a Toyota spokesman said.

Toyota's exports rose 6.2 percent to 1.28 million vehicles in 1996. "Car markets were strong in Europe and Asia last year. Higher shipments to the Middle East were due to the weaker yen," the spokesman said.

The top five carmakers in November forecast the dollar rate for the fiscal year ending in March 1997 would be 106-108 yen compared with 90-96 yen a year earlier. On Monday, the dollar hit a 46-month high of 117.90 yen.

Honda Motor, the third-biggest Japanese car manufacturer in terms of sales value, said that its 1996 domestic output jumped 12.9 percent to 1.09 million vehicles, due to strong domestic demand for new recreational models including the Odyssey, the Step Wagon and the CR-V light sport-utility vehicle.

But its exports fell 14.5 percent to 371,176, despite a resumption of shipments of Civic sedans in the United States in August, and exports of CR-Vs to the United States, which began in December, a Honda spokesman said.

Mazda Motor Corp produced 773,567 vehicles in Japan 1996, up 0.3 percent from a year earlier, reflecting good domestic demand for its Demio compact recreational vehicles. Its exports rose 3.1 percent to 454,125 in 1996, helped by the weaker yen, which makes Japanese exports more competitive overseas.

Such healthy increases in the top carmakers' output would translate into a 1.5 percent rise in overall domestic vehicle production for 1996 to 10.35 million units, the first year-on-year gain in six years, industry sources said.
The full figures, compiled by an industry association, are due to be announced later this month.
But the sources said that Japan's overall vehicle exports are likely to fall 2.1 percent to 3.71 million vehicles in 1996, the eleventh straight year of decline.
Domestic production declined for years as a strong yen forced firms to shift manufacturing offshore to sites with low operating costs and proximity to markets.

Two other major makers, meanwhile, announced falling output. Domestic production at Nissan Motor Co, the second-biggest car maker here, fell six percent to 1.61 million vehicles on waning demand for vehicles launched last year and on poor demand for partially remodelled recreational vehicles.
Exports fell 2.7 percent to 581,854 vehicles in 1996, reflecting slow sales in Europe, a Nissan spokeswoman said.

Mitsubishi Motors Corp, meanwhile, said its 1996 vehicle production fell 9.6 percent from a year earlier to 1.20 million vehicles due to poor demand for sedans and recreational vehicles, while its new Galant sedan and Legnum station wagon enjoyed strong demand because of their economical engine.
Its exports fell 10 percent to 455,498 in 1996, reflecting slow shipments to Europe and the United States because of rising overseas production, a Mitsubishi spokesman said.
